lesson.text: Remember? Young are like their parents but not exactly the same. Today: how those small differences can help some of them survive.
A habitat is the place where a living thing finds food, water and shelter. In a habitat, some living things survive well, some less well, and some cannot survive at all.
A cactus thrives in a hot desert, a fern struggles there, and a fish cannot live there at all. A polar bear's thick fur and fat keep it warm in the Arctic. In a desert it would overheat.
Differences help. A beetle whose colour matches the bark is harder for birds to spot. So it is more likely to live and have young. Colours that help an animal hide are called camouflage.
Differences help animals find food too. A hummingbird with a longer beak reaches deeper into flowers for nectar. And a peacock with the brightest tail is often chosen as a mate.
Habitats change. A pond may dry up in a long drought. A forest may burn or be cut down, and a new road may cut a field in two.
When a habitat changes, living things may stay and cope, or move to a better place. If they can do neither, they die out there. New plants and animals may move in.

People can help. A tunnel under a road lets hedgehogs cross safely. New trees bring birds back, and a fish ladder lets salmon swim past a dam. To judge a plan, ask: does it help, and what does it cost? Next: food, skeletons and muscles.

exercises.hint: Think of a green grasshopper on green grass.
choices: colours that help an animal hide
exercises.explain: Camouflage is colouring that helps an animal blend into its habitat and hide.

exercises.prompt: A green grasshopper is hard to spot on green grass.
exercises.hint: Does its colour match the grass?
exercises.explain: True: its green colour is camouflage.

exercises.prompt: Where does a cactus survive well?
exercises.hint: A cactus stores water in its thick stem.
choices: at the bottom of a lake
exercises.explain: A cactus can store water, so it survives well in a hot, dry desert.

exercises.prompt: What does a habitat give a living thing?
exercises.hint: What does every animal need to live?
exercises.explain: A habitat gives a living thing its food, water and shelter.

exercises.prompt: A fish can survive on dry sand.
exercises.explain: False: a fish needs water to breathe through its gills.

exercises.prompt: Dark moths and pale moths live on dark tree bark. Birds hunt moths. Which moths are more likely to survive?
exercises.hint: Which moth is harder to see on dark bark?
exercises.explain: The dark moths match the dark bark, so birds find them less often.

exercises.prompt: Why does a longer beak help a hummingbird?
choices: It reaches nectar deep in flowers
exercises.explain: A longer beak reaches the nectar deep inside long flowers.

exercises.prompt: A polar bear would survive well in a hot desert.
exercises.hint: Think of its thick fur and fat.
exercises.explain: False: its thick fur and fat keep it warm in the Arctic, but in a hot desert it would overheat.

exercises.prompt: A new road cuts a wood in two. Hedgehogs cannot cross safely. Which plan helps them?
exercises.hint: Which plan lets them cross without meeting cars?
choices: a tunnel under the road for animals
exercises.explain: A wildlife tunnel lets hedgehogs cross under the road safely.

exercises.prompt: A pond dries up in a long drought. Put what happens in order.
items: Grasses grow in the dry mud
exercises.explain: No rain, the pond shrinks, the water animals struggle, and land plants move into the dry mud.

exercises.prompt: Rabbits of one kind have thick or thin fur. The winters get colder. Which are more likely to survive and have young?
exercises.hint: Which fur keeps a rabbit warm?
exercises.explain: Thick fur keeps them warm, so more thick-furred rabbits live to have young.

items: Soon most beetles there are brown
More brown beetles live and have young
Birds spot the green ones on bark
Some beetles are brown, some green
exercises.explain: The beetles differ, birds catch the easy-to-see ones, the hidden ones have young, and their colour spreads.

exercises.prompt: Every change to a habitat is caused by people.
exercises.hint: Think of a flood or a drought.
exercises.explain: False: floods, droughts, storms and fires also change habitats.

exercises.prompt: A frogs' pond was filled in. Which plan is best for the frogs?
exercises.hint: Which plan helps many frogs at a low cost?
choices: Plan A: a new pond nearby
exercises.explain: A new pond nearby helps many frogs and costs little.

exercises.prompt: Beavers build a dam, and a stream becomes a pond. Which animals may move in?
exercises.explain: A new pond is a habitat for water animals like frogs and ducks.

exercises.prompt: Match each living thing to where it survives well.
exercises.hint: Think about what each one needs: water, heat or cold.
exercises.explain: A camel in a hot desert, a polar bear in the icy Arctic, a shark in the sea and a frog in a pond.

exercises.prompt: Which of these help an animal survive in the Arctic?
items: white fur that hides it on snow
exercises.hint: Think of the cold, and of hiding on white snow.
exercises.explain: Thick fur, fat and white fur help in the Arctic. Thin skin and bright colours on snow do not.

exercises.prompt: A habitat has changed. Match each problem to a plan that helps.
items: a road cuts a wood in two
exercises.hint: Each plan should give the animals back what the change took away.
exercises.explain: A tunnel lets animals cross under the road. A fish ladder lets salmon swim past the dam. New trees bring the birds back, and a new pond gives frogs a home again.

exercises.prompt: Which differences help an animal survive in a hot, dry desert?
items: big ears that let heat out
coming out in the cool night
exercises.hint: A desert is hot and has very little water.
exercises.explain: Storing water, big ears that let heat out and coming out at night help in the hot, dry desert. Thick fur and fat would make it overheat, like a polar bear, and there is little water to drink.
